core: The working definition: financial statements are the standardized reports that summarize a business's financial position and performance, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting (Section 2.1) and corroborated by CFI's 3 Financial Statements guide

The three main reports named, each with one line on what it shows and the question it answers: income statement (profit over a period), balance sheet (position at a point in time), cash flow statement (cash movements over a period)
Reading across the three: the statements tell one story from three angles, with an original example (Riverbend Bikes)
The finance view: what lenders, investors, and managers look for in each statement, one line each
Statements and decisions: the numbers become the raw material of finance decisions; financial ratios are a sibling topic, referenced only
The limits: statements describe the past, in accounting terms (the honest note)
The honest framing: statements are a map of the business, not the territory (the reality check)
supporting: Stakeholders as users of financial statements — investors, creditors, employees, managers, regulators, customers, and suppliers — with the common goal of using the statements to make financial decisions; a banker reads them to decide whether to lend (OpenStax Section 2.1)
The complete set of financial statements acting as an X-ray of a company's financial health when evaluated together (OpenStax Section 2.1)

The interrelation of the statements: net income from the income statement flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet, and the balance sheet's cash balance ties to the cash flow statement (OpenStax Principles of Finance Section 5.3; CFI)
The accounting subject owns how the statements are prepared; this lesson references preparation only (accounting sibling lessons)
outOfScope: Preparing the statements (the accounting subject's territory: accounting:foundations:income-statement, accounting:foundations:balance-sheet, accounting:foundations:statement-of-cash-flows; referenced only)
Financial ratios and their calculation (sibling topic: finance:foundations:financial-ratios; referenced only)
Cash flow analysis in depth (sibling topic: finance:foundations:cash-flow; referenced only)
The statement of owner's equity and other statements (named only, not taught here)

claims.claim: Financial statements are the standardized reports that summarize a business's financial position and performance; the complete set of financial statements acts as an X-ray of a company's financial health.

The three main financial statements are the income statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement; together they provide a complete view of performance, financial position, and cash generation.

The income statement shows the revenues and expenses of a business over a period of time and is used to assess profitability and growth; net income, the bottom line, reflects the net impact of the firm's financial transactions.
The balance sheet shows a company's assets, liabilities, and shareholders' equity at a particular point in time — a snapshot — and the two sides must balance.
The cash flow statement shows cash movements from operating, investing, and financing activities over a period of time.
The three statements interrelate: net income from the income statement flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet, and the balance sheet's cash balance ties to the cash flow statement.

Stakeholders — investors, creditors, employees, managers, regulators, customers, and suppliers — use the financial statements to make financial decisions; a banker reads them to decide whether to lend, and management uses the information to make strategic short- and long-term decisions.

The statements are expressed over periods that have already ended (income statement and cash flow statement) or at a single past date (balance sheet), so they describe the past in accounting terms; the honest framing is that statements are a map of the business, not the territory.

conflictingEvidence: None found across the sources used. OpenStax Principles of Accounting and OpenStax Principles of Finance agree with CFI on the identity and one-line purposes of the three statements. The only structural difference: OpenStax's accounting text treats the statement of owner's equity as a fourth major statement; this lesson names it only in passing and does not teach it.
rightsIssues: All sources used as reference; the working definition is paraphrased with attribution to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting (Section 2.1). No source prose reproduced; all examples are original (Riverbend Bikes and Northgate Print Shop are fictional companies).

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Chapter 5, Section 5.1: The Income Statement
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read via Internet Archive capture (openstax.org blocks curl). Supports the finance view of the income statement: it lets financial statement users understand the sales generated during the period and the expenses incurred to generate those sales; if expenses are smaller than sales the result is net income; net income is commonly called the bottom line and reflects the net impact of all financial transactions; the statement is divided into time periods. Facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read via Internet Archive capture. Supports the interrelation of the statements: net income increases retained earnings, dividends reduce it, and the retained earnings balance is then reflected on the balance sheet; the connections between the balance sheet and the income statement are depicted as a flow. Facts synthesized into original prose.
